claim: Across 16 open-weight models, adding a concrete rule (naming a command/path/identifier) to a SKILL.md raises single-answer directive compliance by an average of +0.41.
stance_target: SOPs-to-Agent-Skills pillar — specific rule content in Skills measurably changes agent behavior, not just SOP framing
scope_conditions: 16 open-weight instruction-tuned models, 3.8B-32B parameters, 300-probe main set
quoted_support: Across 16 open-weight models, an added rule raises compliance in a single answer by +0.41 on average.

claim: In a multi-step sandbox using four agents, a Skill revision raised the required-action rate by +0.23 on average and blind-human-judged final correctness by +0.10 on average.
stance_target: Rigid evals / quality control pillar — measurable, reproducible effect of Skill content on agent task success in a real sandbox, not just single-turn compliance
scope_conditions: mini-SWE-agent scaffold, network-less sandbox, 80 executable tasks, Qwen 3.5-9B/27B, Devstral-Small-2507, Claude Sonnet 4.5
quoted_support: Across the four agents, the rate at which the agent takes the required action rises by +0.23 on average (+0.16 to +0.36), and for the three agents that blind judges assessed, final correctness rises by +0.10 on average (+0.06 to +0.14).

claim: On-demand Skill loading (real progressive disclosure, where the agent decides whether to read the Skill body) preserves only about 51% of the action-rate gain for the four tested agents and about 38% for the three open models, compared to having the Skill body preloaded in the prompt.
stance_target: Triggers/Infrastructure pillar — progressive disclosure (Anthropic's recommended context-isolation design) trades agent effectiveness for token efficiency, a real cost
scope_conditions: sandbox agents, on-demand Skill loading condition vs preloaded condition
quoted_support: Real tools load a Skill's body only when the agent decides it needs it. In that setting the four agents keep about half of the action gain on average (51%), and the three open models about 38%.

claim: Loading a Skill's body at all (carrying cost vs. name/description only) raises agent-episode token consumption by 37-57%, with a 50% average increase, while a revision to an already-loaded Skill adds no detectable marginal cost inside an agent episode.
stance_target: Cost & Resource Optimization pillar — quantified token overhead of Skill-body loading vs. revision cost, directly informing subscription/API economics modeling
scope_conditions: multi-step agent episodes, token measurement under each model's own tokenizer
quoted_support: Inside an agent episode we could not detect extra cost from the revision, while loading the Skill body at all adds 37 to 57% more tokens.
numbers: 37-57% token increase from loading Skill body
17-27% more tokens per single-step request after a revision

claim: One in five (20%) rule-model pairs show the prompt growing from an added rule with no detectable compliance gain, i.e., direct evidence of wasted token spend from over-specified Skill content.
stance_target: Cost & Resource Optimization pillar — adding rules to Skills is not free; a meaningful fraction burns tokens without benefit
scope_conditions: rule-model pairs, 5 samples per condition, compliance measured in 0.2 steps
quoted_support: In 20%, the prompt grows but we detect no change in compliance, and we call these [null gains].
numbers: 20% of rule-model pairs show no detectable gain

claim: Skill revisions change harness-configuration files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor/Codex configs, Claude Code agent/command definitions) more often than size-matched non-Skill commits in the same repository, and creating a new Skill couples even more tightly to harness changes.
stance_target: Open Source Architecture Reading pillar — Skills and harness/agent configuration co-evolve and should be reviewed/versioned together, not treated as independent artifacts
scope_conditions: 6,955 revision commits across 855 re-cloned repositories, matched by repository and commit-size band
quoted_support: Matched on repository and files changed, 23.0% of revision commits and 18.5% of other commits change harness configuration, a difference of +4.5 points... Of the creation commits, 36.7% change harness configuration, against 21.8% of matched commits (+14.8 points).

claim: Deleting a rule from a Skill lowers compliance with it by 0.27-0.33 across 8 tested models, roughly three-quarters the magnitude of the gain from adding the same rule, and deleting a 'replaced' rule has far larger negative effect (-0.58) than deleting a mere duplicate (-0.12).
stance_target: Rigid evals pillar — Skill deletions are not symmetric/neutral; removing superseding rules without replacement is a quality-control risk
scope_conditions: 8 models (6 Qwen, Phi-4-mini, OLMo-2), hand-checked deletion reasons
quoted_support: Removing a rule lowers compliance with it by 0.27-0.33 on each of eight models... deleting a duplicate changes compliance by -0.12 (n=27) and deleting a replaced rule by -0.58 (n=24).
numbers: -0.27 to -0.33 compliance drop from rule deletion

claim: The benefit of adding a new rule to a Skill declines as the Skill occupies more of the model's usable context window, falling from +0.424 compliance gain at low Skill occupancy to +0.270 when the Skill fills three-quarters of the context window.
stance_target: Context isolation / context engineering pillar — Skill size directly trades off against rule effectiveness, motivating tight context budgets per Skill
scope_conditions: occupancy groups defined as ratio of Skill tokens to model's usable context window
quoted_support: Across occupancy groups it falls from 0.424 at low occupancy to 0.270 when the Skill fills three quarters of the window.
numbers: +0.424 compliance gain at low Skill occupancy

claim: Maintainers almost never document a model-related motive when revising a Skill: only 0.4% of commit subjects name a model version, and just 4.2% of hand-labelled commits target a model or platform.
stance_target: Open source architecture reading pillar — Skill maintenance history provides limited signal about which model generation a rule was tuned for
quoted_support: The repository history rarely documents a model-related motive. Only 0.4% of commit subjects name a model version, 4.2% of 120 hand-labelled commits target a model or platform.
numbers: 0.4% of commit subjects name a model version
3.3% of pairs add/change a versioned model name
